data.title: Nevus spilus (speckled lentiginous nevus) — viva
data.summary: Nevi & hamartomas · 14 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Nevus spilus (speckled lentiginous nevus)** (Nevi & hamartomas)_

**Q1. What is nevus spilus?**
- Speckled lentiginous naevus: a light-brown café-au-lait-like background patch studded with darker brown-black macules or papules (lentigines, junctional/compound naevi, sometimes blue or Spitz naevi); present at birth or appearing in childhood; considered a type of congenital melanocytic naevus (HRAS/BRAF mosaic)

**Q2. Clinical types.**
- Macular type (flat speckles — lentigines/junctional naevi) and papular type (raised speckles — compound/dermal naevi)
- Size from small to giant/segmental (zosteriform)
- Phacomatosis pigmentokeratotica (papular nevus spilus + nevus sebaceous — HRAS), phacomatosis pigmentovascularis (with vascular malformation), speckled lentiginous naevus syndrome (neurological anomalies)

**Q3. Malignant potential.**
- Low; melanoma reported especially in large/giant or segmental lesions and the papular type — monitor speckles for change; biopsy atypical components

**Q4. Differential diagnosis.**
- Café-au-lait macule with lentigines (NF1/Legius — axillary freckling), agminated lentigines/naevi, congenital melanocytic naevus, Becker's naevus, partial unilateral lentiginosis, LEOPARD/Noonan

**Q5. Management.**
- Observation with photographs and dermoscopy; excision of any atypical speckle
- Cosmetic: Q-switched/picosecond lasers (background and speckles), excision of small lesions; caution — laser may complicate monitoring

**Q6. Histopathology.**
- Background macule: lentigo-simplex-like basal hyperpigmentation with slightly increased melanocytes; dark speckles: junctional, compound or intradermal naevi, sometimes Spitz/blue naevi

**Q7. What is phacomatosis pigmentokeratotica?**
- Co-existence of speckled lentiginous naevus (papular type) and nevus sebaceous (HRAS mosaicism), sometimes with neurological and skeletal anomalies

**Q8. What is phacomatosis pigmentovascularis?**
- Co-existence of vascular malformation (port-wine stain/ cutis marmorata) with pigmentary naevi — dermal melanocytosis (cesioflammea), nevus spilus (spilorosea), or both; GNA11/GNAQ mosaicism; may have Sturge–Weber/KT features

**Q9. How should you follow a large nevus spilus?**
- Photography and dermoscopy annually; examine dark speckles for change; biopsy any enlarging, irregular or nodular area — melanoma risk is low but higher in large/zosteriform/papular types

**Q10. Describe the clinical presentation.**
- Tan CALM-like background patch (present at birth or early childhood) with numerous smaller darker brown-black macules/ papules ('speckles') developing over time; 1–20 cm; trunk and limbs; may be zosteriform/ segmental

**Q11. Macular vs papular types.**
- Macular type: speckles are flat (lentigines/ junctional naevi) — associated with phacomatosis pigmentovascularis
- Papular type: speckles are raised (compound/ intradermal naevi) — associated with phacomatosis pigmentokeratotica; possibly slightly higher melanoma risk

**Q12. Genetics.**
- Post-zygotic HRAS (papular) and other RAS/ RAF mosaic mutations — explaining the clonal background and speckles

**Q13. Lasers in nevus spilus.**
- Q-switched/ picosecond lasers lighten background and speckles (variable, recurrence); avoid treating atypical speckles without histology; follow-up for changes

**Q14. Describe melanoma types and Breslow/ Clark levels (often linked question).**
- Types: superficial spreading (commonest in West), nodular, lentigo maligna melanoma, acral lentiginous (commonest in Indians — soles, palms, nails), mucosal, desmoplastic, amelanotic
- Breslow thickness (mm, from granular layer to deepest cell) — main prognostic factor: T1 ≤1 mm, T2 1–2, T3 2–4, T4 >4 mm (a/b by ulceration); Clark levels I–V (anatomical) now largely replaced
- Margins: in situ 0.5–1 cm, ≤1 mm 1 cm, 1–2 mm 1–2 cm, >2 mm 2 cm; sentinel node biopsy for >0.8 mm or ulcerated

## Quick spotter facts
- Café-au-lait patch with dark speckles — nevus spilus

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Melanocytic naevi). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
